abstract: "Sequence-space synaesthesia is a perceptual condition in which ordinal sequences (e.g., numbers, days of the week, or months of the year) are experienced at specific spatial locations. This perceptual condition is commonly identified using self-reports (e.g. questionnaires) and behavioural consistency test methods. Existing consistency methods measure the spatial distance between responses to repeated stimuli but ignore the ordinal and geometric properties of spatial forms. This Registered Report consists of an exploratory Phase I and a confirmatory registered Phase II. In Phase I, we evaluated established and novel consistency metrics in an aggregated sample of 685 participants from four independent datasets (396 self-reported synaesthetes and 289 controls). Established metrics quantified the distance between repeated responses to the same stimulus. Novel metrics used geospatial tools to represent each ordered sequence as a line or polygon and to quantify self-intersections, topological simplicity, validity and compactness. Receiver operating characteristic analyses indicated that permuted topological validity (AUC = 80.96%) and Polsby-Popper compactness score (AUC = 78.92%) did not significantly differ from standardised within-stimulus perimeter (AUC = 78.81%). In Phase II, we will examine the predictive validity of the metrics with an AUC of at least 75% in an independent dataset. Phase I suggests the relevance of topological principles for sequence-space representations and aims to optimise consistency tests to detect SSS."

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Sequence-Space Synaesthesia (SSS), or visuo-spatial forms, is the
phenomenon where people visualise ordinal sequences occupying specific
spatial positions. For example, numbers, weekdays or months (i.e.
inducers) are experienced as arranged in an ellipse, zigzag, curved line
or other idiosyncratic configurations [@galton1880; @flournoy1893]. The
experienced location or configuration is the concurrent. Spatial forms
can differ across individuals and inducer categories, however within
person inducer-concurrent mappings are described as automatic and
consistent over time [@seron1992; @deroy2013]. Current consistency tasks
operationalise consistency by measuring repeated spatial responses.
Consistency metrics are then extracted to estimate the variability or
distance between repeated responses. However, current metrics for
classifying SSS from consistency-task data have important limitations
[@brang2010; @rothen2016; @ward2022; @ward2018; @eagleman2007;
@sagiv2006; @baron-cohen1987]. The present Registered Report therefore
uses an exploratory *Phase I* to optimise consistency methods on
available data. In the confirmatory *Phase II*, the optimal methods will
be tested on new data. Consistency metrics face the challenge of
developing a single metric capable of correctly testing multiple forms.

## Testing Consistency {#sec-consistency-tests}

Spatial forms are heterogeneous but consistent. They may be experienced
in two or three-dimensional arrangements [@eagleman2009a; @price2013],
in external (projector) or within an internal egocentric space
(associator) [@dixon2004; @smilek2007], and from perspectives that can
be zoomed, rotated, or shifted at will [@gould2014; @jarick2009].
Lastly, their shapes also vary, including lines, ovals, loops and
zigzags. With some recurring shapes being more frequent, for example,
month forms are often oval [@eagleman2009a]. Despite the heterogeneity
in dimensionality, reference frame, and shape, consistency tasks are
objective measures for repeated response variability in time: repeated
presentation of the same inducer should elicit comparable spatial
responses for synaesthetes. However, several limitations have been
identified for current consistency metrics.

SSS is usually identified using phenomenological self-reports and
consistency tasks. Questionnaires assess consistency, automaticity,
directionality, and developmental onset. Consistency tasks assess the
stability of inducer-concurrent mapping by repeatedly presenting each
inducer and quantifying the variability of the corresponding responses
[@rothen2013a; @rothen2016]. Lower variability is interpreted as greater
consistency because synaesthetes can respond from their perceptual
experience while non-synaesthetes can only be consistent by relying on a
memorisation strategy. In grapheme-colour synaesthesia (GCS), for
example, repeated colour selections for the same grapheme are compared
in colour space [@rothen2013a]. An analogous rationale has been applied
to SSS by comparing repeated spatial responses. However, existing SSS
tasks discriminate self-reported synaesthetes from controls less
accurately than established grapheme-colour tasks, see @tbl-01.

::: {#tbl-01}
|             |                              |                             |
|:-----------:|:----------------------------:|:---------------------------:|
|             | Grapheme-Colour Synaesthesia | Sequence-Space Synaesthesia |
|             |        [@rothen2013a]        |        [@rothen2016]        |
|     AUC     |             93%              |             76%             |
| Sensitivity |             90%              |             88%             |
| Specificity |             94%              |             77%             |

: Consistency task performance for grapheme-colour and sequence-space
synaesthesia. AUC = Area Under the Curve.
:::

In the SSS consistency task, participants complete multiple
presentations of digits, weekdays, and months and click the screen
location associated with each inducer/stimulus. The resulting responses
are then used to test participants' consistency with consistency
metrics. @brang2010, for example, evaluated the distance between
repeated responses to the same inducer (e.g. January and January)
relative to the distance between adjacent inducers (e.g. February). A
response was defined as consistent if it fell within 1.96 *z-scores*.
Their criterion however identified only 4 of 81 self-reported
synaesthetes and may therefore have been too conservative. @rothen2016
connected the three responses to the same inducer (e.g. the three clicks
for January) into a triangle and calculated its area and perimeter;
smaller triangles indicate more consistent responses. They proposed
classifying participants as SSS when the mean triangle area was smaller
than 0.203% of the screen area (see also @ward2018). This is currently
the most widely used metric to test for genuine SSS.

## Limitations of Current Consistency Metrics

Current consistency tests have limitations. First, a participant can
obtain an artificially high consistency score by repeatedly clicking on
the same spatial location for every stimulus [@rothen2016]. In SSS,
exclusion via visual inspection of these responses improved
classification performances of the triangle area metric (i.e. Area Under
the Curve = 85%, sensitivity = 87%, specificity = 81%; see @rothen2016).

Second, certain consistency metrics may favour certain spatial forms
[@ward2018]. Linear or highly regular forms, including elliptical month
forms, may perform differently from irregular forms when considering
only the distance between responses to repeated stimuli [@flournoy1893;
@eagleman2009a; @brang2010]. This has led to including additional
criteria such as adding standard deviation combined with questionnaire
cut-off [@ward2018] and the comparison of individual scores with chance
level permutation-based distributions in GCS [@root2021] and SSS
[@ward2022a].

Third, current consistency tests treat each inducer independently and
therefore ignore the ordinal relationship among inducers. Inducers
follow an ordered path or form (e.g. Monday `→` Tuesday `→` Wednesday,
etc.), where ordinal information is central to sequence processing of
numbers [@lyons2013]. Furthermore, previous SSS research has
investigated metrics of adjacent inducer-concurrent pairs such as
distances [@brang2010] or angles [@eagleman2009a]. Number forms may
likewise be constructed from ordinal relations [@tang2008]. A form-level
metric considering the spatial ordinal arrangement of all the stimuli
within a certain category (i.e. weekdays or months) can therefore assess
the coherence of these spatial forms rather than the variability between
repetitions of the same stimuli.

Fourth, number responses may reflect spatial-numerical associations that
also occur in the general population. The spatial-numerical association
of response codes (SNARC) effect describes faster left-hand responses to
smaller numbers and faster right-hand responses to larger numbers
[@dehaene1993; @hubbard2005a]. At the group level, the SNARC effect is
robust and has been taken as evidence for an implicit left-to-right
spatial representation of numbers (mental number line). Its reliability
at the individual level is lower [@cipora2019; @ramos2026], and its
origin remains debated [@bassomoro2018; @keus2005]. Nevertheless, a
widespread left-to-right mental number line could help non-synaesthetes
respond consistently to numbers, making number responses less diagnostic
than weekday or month responses.

## Present Study {#sec-present-study}

These limitations motivate comparing stimulus-level and form-level
consistency metrics. Stimulus-level metrics, such as distance, area and
perimeter, describe the variability of repeated responses to one
stimulus. Form-level metrics instead describe the whole ordered path of
a sequence category (e.g. Monday to Sunday) within one repetition. We
used cartography tools to represent each path as a line or polygon and
to quantify its topological properties: whether the path crosses itself
(self-intersection), whether the polygon is simple and valid according
to geographic standards, and how compact it is. We expected
synaesthetes' forms to cross themselves less often and to be more often
valid and compact than controls' forms.

This Registered Report consists of two phases. The present *Phase I* is
an exploratory analysis merging four available datasets on consistency
tasks to find the optimal consistency metrics. *Phase II* will be a
confirmatory evaluation of the consistency metrics in an independent
dataset of consistency tasks.

*Phase I* had three aims. First, we reproduced established
stimulus-level consistency metrics such as area and perimeter formed by
repeated responses to each stimulus. Second, we constructed ordered
paths (segments) and polygons for each sequence category and evaluated
topological form-level metrics, see @fig-01. Third, we compared all the
metrics using receiver operating characteristics (ROC) analyses based on
self-reported SSS and control groups. We selected the optimal metrics
based on the AUC. We retained metrics with an AUC of at least 75% for
*Phase II* validation.

In *Phase II*, we will evaluate whether the metrics and cutoffs
generalise and are validated in an independent dataset that has not yet
been analysed (@sachdeva2024, Stage 1 in-principle acceptance,
<https://osf.io/6wn4m>).

```{r Load data}
# In the following I upload and merge the data from Ward, Rothen and Van Peters. Data is stored into a full dataset ds (i.e. 1 row per trial) and a dataset per participant ds_Quest (i.e. 1 row per participant).

###  Ward Data
ds_syn       <- read_excel("Data/raw_synaesthetes_consistency_anon.xlsx")
ds_syn$group <- "Syn"
ds_ctl       <- read_excel("Data/raw_controls_consistency_anon.xlsx")
ds_ctl$group <- "Ctl"

ds_Q_syn       <- read_excel("Data/raw_synaesthetes_questionnaire_anon.xlsx")
ds_Q_syn$group <- "Syn"
ds_Q_ctl       <- read_excel("Data/raw_controls_questionnaire_anon.xlsx")

# Merge wards datafiles:
ds <- merge(ds_syn,ds_ctl, all = TRUE)
ds_Q <- merge(ds_Q_syn,ds_Q_ctl, all = TRUE)

# Ward only uses those who completed the Questionnaire (i.e. N = 215+252 = 467)

  filter(session_id %in% unique(ds_Q$session_id))
 
### Rothen Data

### Rename variables to match datasets

ds_Q$...37 <- NULL

ds_Q$SD_simulation <- NULL

ds$ID <- ds$session_id
ds_Q$ID <- ds_Q$session_id

ds_Q$dataSource <- "Ward"

# From Rothen:

ds_Rothen$dataSource <- "Rothen"

# From the paper (all the same since lab based):
ds_Rothen$width  <- 1024
ds_Rothen$height <- 768
```

```{r MergeWard2}
# This data was provided by Jamie by mail. The data is prepared in a separeate file

ds_Ward2$Cond[ds_Ward2$stimulus %in% c("Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Friday","Saturday","Sunday")] <- "weekday"
ds_Ward2$Cond[ds_Ward2$stimulus %in% c("January", "February", "March", "April", "May","June","July","August","September","October","November","December")] <- "month"

# Now I somehow need to define the groups
# If a response in the questionnaire then syn, if not then control.
ds_Ward2$group <- NaN
ds_Ward2$group[is.na(ds_Ward2$`Q1 . Some people routinely think about sequences as arranged in a particular spatial configuration (as in the examples below), do you think this might apply to you? (1=strongly agree, 5= strongly disagree)`)] <- "Ctl"
ds_Ward2$group[!is.na(ds_Ward2$`Q1 . Some people routinely think about sequences as arranged in a particular spatial configuration (as in the examples below), do you think this might apply to you? (1=strongly agree, 5= strongly disagree)`)] <- "Syn"

ds_Ward2_Q$`questionnaire score` <- ds_Ward2_Q[,4] +

ds_Q       <- merge(ds_Q,ds_Ward2_Q,all = TRUE)
```

```{r Wrangle data}
# Now we can enrich our dataset and process  several checks
# Add Condition, i.e. stim type:
ds$Cond <- NaN
ds$Cond[ds$stimulus %in% c("1","2","3","4","5","6","7","8","9","0")] <- "number"
ds$Cond[ds$stimulus %in% c("Monday","Tuesday","Wednesday","Thursday","Friday","Saturday","Sunday")] <- "weekday"
ds$Cond[ds$stimulus %in% c("January", "February", "March", "April", "May","June","July","August","September","October","November","December")] <- "month"

# Add stimulus repetition number
ds <- ds %>%
  group_by(ID, stimulus) %>%
  arrange(ID, stimulus, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  mutate(repetition = row_number()) %>%
  ungroup()

# few trials that have more than 3 repetitions somehow:
ds <- ds %>% filter(repetition <= 3)

# Factorialize group variable to avoid confusions:
ds$group   <- as.factor(ds$group)
ds_Q$group <- as.factor(ds_Q$group)
```

```{r, FilterTrials}
# This is potentially a critical part for the results. Need to decide:
# (1) how to treat same coordinate responses, i.e. when ID clicks on the same position (see also Rothen and Ward)
# (2) how to treat missing data (i.e. NA & NaN)

# For (1), since z-score might fail (i.e. if all same coordinates) -->  turn same coordinates to NaN
# For (2), since sf does not accept missing data -->  we exclude those responses.
# This leads to some stimuli having only 2 repetitions (i.e. ID %in% 4_JB) AND some ID having to few pairs.
# Since polygons need at least 4 coordinate pairs. --> check enough data per repetition

# Important. To reproduce Rothen, the X = -1 and Y = -1 need to be interpreted as missing data (NaN):
ds$x[ds$x == -1] <- NaN
ds$y[ds$y == -1] <- NaN

# Detect ID has the same coordinates across Conditions:
ds <- ds %>%
    group_by(ID, Cond) %>% 
    mutate(SameCoord_x = length(unique(x[!is.na(x)])) == 1,SameCoord_y = length(unique(y[!is.na(y)])) == 1)

# NaNification:
ds$x[ds$SameCoord_x] <- NaN
ds$y[ds$SameCoord_y] <- NaN
ds$x[is.na(ds$x)]    <- NaN  # In VanPeters, some NA data all as NaN
ds$y[is.na(ds$y)]    <- NaN 

N1 <- length(unique(ds$ID)) # Track if ID loss

# Remove NaN from the dataset:
All_n <- length(ds$x) # Track trial loss
ds <- ds %>%
  filter(!is.na(x))
ds <- ds %>%
  filter(!is.na(y))
All_n2 <- length(ds$x)

N2 <- length(unique(ds$ID))  # Track if ID loss

# Check that each stimulus has 3 repetitions (3+2+1 = 6).
ds <- ds %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    group_by(ID, stimulus) %>%
    mutate(SumRep = sum(repetition)== 6)

ds <- ds[ds$SumRep,]
All_n3<- length(ds$x)

# Counts how many full conditions each ID has (should be 3):
tmp2 <- ds %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(ID, Cond, repetition) %>%
  filter(row_number() == 1) %>%
  reframe(ntrials = length(x)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(ID) %>%
  reframe(nCond = sum(ntrials)/3)

# Later on, we make polygons. These need at least 4 points. Hence we exclude ID's with less than 4 responses per condition:
tmp <- ds %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  group_by(ID, Cond, repetition) %>%
  reframe(ntrials = length(x))

ds <- ds %>%
  filter(!ID %in% tmp$ID[tmp$ntrials < 4])

N3 <- length(unique(ds$ID))

# Match ID to ds_Q:
IDlist <- unique(ds$ID)
ds_Q <- ds_Q %>%
  filter(ID %in% IDlist)
```

# Methods - Phase I

The code and data required to reproduce analyses and the present
manuscript are available at
<https://github.com/remLach/SpaceSequenceSynDiagnostic>. All the
analyses were conducted in R, using the following packages:
`r pakret::pkrt_list("tidyr", "dplyr")` for data wrangling,
`r pakret::pkrt_list("sf")` for geographical feature extractions,
`r pakret::pkrt_list("pROC")` for ROC analyses and
`r pakret::pkrt_list("ggplot2", "ggVennDiagram", "ggridges", "ggforce", "cowplot", "corrplot")`
for figures.

## Datasets and Participants

We searched for accessible datasets that administered the same
consistency tasks to self-reported synaesthetes and controls. Four
datasets met this criterion. Two datasets were collected in laboratory:
@rothen2016 (see also
[https://osf.io/6hq94](https://osf.io/6hq94/files/osfstorage)) and
@vanpetersen2020 (see also
<https://data.ru.nl/collections/di/dcc/DSC_2018.00019_653>). The two
others were collected online: @ward2022a (see also
<https://osf.io/nu5v4>) and an additional unpublished dataset was
provided by Jamie Ward (private communication, October 2025).

Before merging the datasets, the stimuli of @vanpetersen2020 were
translated from Dutch to English. For the number category we excluded
digits different from 0-9; i.e. the stimuli 50 and 100 from
@vanpetersen2020. After merging the datasets, we applied minimal
pre-processing, resulting in a final sample of `r N3` from the initial
`r N1` participants. Empty, skipped trials and trials flagged for having
the same x or y coordinates across categories and repetitions were
excluded, representing `r round(100 * (All_n - All_n2)/All_n, 2)`% of
all trials. This resulted in the exclusion of `r N1 - N2` participants.
A further `r All_n2 - All_n3` trials were removed because the stimulus
no longer had all three repetitions. Then `r N2 - N3` additional
participants were excluded for having fewer than four responses in a
category and repetition, the minimum required to construct polygons.
Among the retained participants, `r sum(tmp2$nCond < 3)` were missing at
least one category by repetition form. The final sample consisted of
`r sum(ds_Q$group == "Syn")` self-reported synaesthetes and
`r sum(ds_Q$group == "Ctl")` self-reported controls, see @tbl-02.

::: {#tbl-02}
|  |  |  |  |  |
|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|:-------------:|
|  | SSS |  | Controls |  |
|  | N | Age | N | Age |
| [@rothen2016] | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "Rothen" & ds_Q$group == "Syn")` | 23.1 | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "Rothen" & ds_Q$group == "Ctl")` | 28.2 |
| [@ward2022a] | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "Ward" & ds_Q$group == "Syn")` | 37.3 | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "Ward" & ds_Q$group == "Ctl")` | 19.9 |
| [@vanpetersen2020] | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "PeterCor" & ds_Q$group == "Syn")` | 23.2 | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "PeterCor" & ds_Q$group == "Ctl")` | 21.6 |
| Ward, unpublished | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "Ward2" & ds_Q$group == "Syn")` | NA | `r sum(ds_Q$dataSource == "Ward2" & ds_Q$group == "Ctl")` | NA |
| **Total** | **`r sum(ds_Q$group == "Syn")`** |  | **`r sum(ds_Q$group == "Ctl")`** |  |

: Descriptives of each dataset.
:::

Detailed questionnaire data were available only for the two datasets
provided by Jamie Ward, which together included
`r sum(ds_Q$dataSource %in% c("Ward","Ward2"))` participants. @fig-apx00
summarises self-reported SSS for the stimulus categories used in the
consistency test (i.e. number, weekdays and month) of Ward datasets .

## Procedure

For the consistency task, on each trial, a stimulus appeared centrally
on the screen. Participants clicked the location at which they
visualised that stimulus. Stimuli were presented sequentially in random
order. Participants in the @vanpetersen2020 and @rothen2016 datasets
could skip trials.

Stimuli included seven weekdays (Monday - Sunday), 12 months (January -
December) and 10 numbers (0 - 9). Each stimulus was presented three
times (i.e. three repetitions). In the two Ward datasets, presentation
order was randomised with the constraint that all 29 unique stimuli
appeared once before any stimulus was repeated. Across participants, the
median display resolution was `r median(ds$width)` X
`r median(ds$height)` (minimum of `r min(ds$width)` X
`r min(ds$height)`, and a maximum of `r max(ds$width)` X
`r max(ds$height)`).

## Consistency Methods and Analyses

The analysis on the merged dataset proceeded in five steps. First, we
reproduced stimulus-level area and perimeter metrics. Second, we ordered
coordinates by sequence category and repetition to construct paths and
polygons. Third, we calculated geometric and topological form-level
metrics. Fourth, for selected form-level metrics, we permuted repetition
labels across stimuli to assess stability across repetitions. Fifth, we
compared the discrimination of all metrics with ROC analyses and
examined robustness across datasets and questionnaire-score subsamples.

### Reproduced Consistency Metrics

We reproduced two existing consistency methods of the spatial
variability of responses to the same stimulus: triangle area and
perimeter [@rothen2016; @ward2022a; @vanpetersen2020]. A participant
with a stable inducer-concurrent mapping should place the three
responses to a stimulus close together. Smaller areas and perimeters
therefore indicate greater within-stimulus consistency (@fig-01 A).

For each stimulus, the three response coordinates, one per repetition,
*(x1, y1), (x2, y2)* and *(x3, y3)*, defined a triangle. Area and
perimeter were calculated using [@eq-area] and [@eq-perim],
respectively. We averaged each stimulus-level score per participant.
Triangle area was expressed as a percentage of screen area to permit
comparison across display sizes. To account for screen size and spread
variability, we also calculated triangle area and perimeter after
standardising (*z-score*) each participant’s x and y coordinates.
Standardisation was applied within each participant’s trials, separately
for the x and the y axis. Area and perimeter computed from standardised
coordinates are therefore expressed in units of standardised
coordinates, not as z-scores of the metric.

$$Area = \frac{|x1y2  +  x2y3  +  x3y1 \mathbin{-} x1y3 \mathbin{-}  x2y1 \mathbin{-} x3y2|}{2}$$ {#eq-area}

$$\begin{split}
Perimeter = \sqrt{(x2 \mathbin{-} x1)^2 + (y2 \mathbin{-} y1)^2} + \\ \sqrt{(x3 \mathbin{-} x2)^2 + (y3 \mathbin{-} y2)^2} + \\ \sqrt{(x1 \mathbin{-}  x3)^2 + (y1 \mathbin{-} y3)^2}
\end{split}$$ {#eq-perim}

For example, three close responses to Monday will result in a small
triangle area and perimeter. A recognised limitation of this method is
that clicking the same position for every stimulus also produces
near-zero values, therefore resulting in artificially high consistency
(see for example the first four rows of @fig-03).

![Examples of extreme scores on each consistency
metric](fig-03.png){#fig-03
apa-note="Each row represents one metric. For each sequence category, the left panels show the participant with the most control-like score and the right panels show the participant with the most SSS-like score. The direction of the classification differs across metrics."
width="600"}

### Form-Level and Topological Metrics

For each sequence category, we ordered stimuli according to their
ordinal position (e.g. 0 `→`1`→`2`→`3`→` ... `→`9) and connected the
corresponding coordinates within each repetition. Each participant
therefore contributed up to three forms per category and nine forms in
total. A metric for each form was then extracted using different methods
that will be described later.

Each form was represented by the ordered responses as an open segment or
closed polygon. For polygon-based metrics, we closed the path by
connecting the final stimulus to the first. Hence the form was
represented as segments or polygons in a two-dimensional Cartesian
plane, see @fig-01. This was done using `r pakret::pkrt("sf")` to
construct segments (i.e. line strings) and polygons from participants’
coordinates. The same package was used to compute geometric and
topological features.

For example, @fig-01 illustrates the procedure for weekday forms. Three
polygons are created by connecting the responses of Monday-Sunday as a
closed path within each repetition. Polygon-based metrics and properties
are then calculated. In the permutation analysis, the response assigned
to each weekday is randomly drawn from the repetitions.

#### Segment Self-intersections

The self-intersection metric counted self-crossings of each segment
separately. We expected less organised responses from controls to lead
to more self-intersection than SSS responses. When the segments include
the same coordinates, this is counted as one intersection. More
intersections push towards control classification, hence solving the
problem of participants clicking the same points.

For each category and repetition, we counted the number of times the
segment path of consecutive stimuli intersected itself. Counts were
calculated for all available category-by-repetition forms and then
averaged within participant.

For example, @fig-04 illustrates the self-intersection count for one
participant across three sequence categories (columns) and three
repetitions (rows). This participant’s mean self-intersection score was
$((4+1+2)+(2+1+0)+(3+0+0))/9 = 1.44$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-04
#| fig-cap: Example self-intersections test
#| out-width: "60%"
#| apa-note: "Average of the total number of self-intersections across repetitions and categories. In this example participant, the score is 1.44"
#| fig-align: center

knitr::include_graphics("Fig04.pdf")
```

#### Topological Simplicity and Validity

Topological properties characterise a geometry’s conformity to
predefined rules of spatial structure and relationships. We expected SSS
forms to follow topological rules. We reasoned and used a cartographic
analogy: as a map representation of a territory is constrained by its
geographical physical reality which follows topological rules, SSS
spatial forms could be constrained by similar topological rules.

Topological simplicity evaluates whether a geometric object has a simple
structure without self-intersections or self-tangencies. According to
the Open Geospatial Consortium (OGC) Simple Features Specification
[@herring2010], a polygon boundary is simple if it does not pass through
the same point more than once [@postgis].

Topological validity indicates if a polygon is well-formed and valid
according to the OGC Simple Features Specification [@herring2010].
Requirements include: (1) polygon rings are simple (i.e., they do not
touch or self-intersect), (2) boundary rings do not cross, (3) boundary
rings only touch points tangentially, (4) rings that define holes are
contained within the exterior ring, and (5) the polygon rings must not
split the polygon [@herring2010]. Note that simplicity is a condition
for validity: a polygon may be simple yet invalid.

Each form received a binary score for simplicity and validity (1 =
simple or valid, 0 = complex or invalid). Scores were averaged across
the available forms (up to three categories × three repetitions),
resulting in scores ranging from 0 to 1, with higher values expected for
synaesthetes. A score of 1 indicates that all available forms were
valid; a score of 0 indicates that none were valid. For example, if all
three weekday polygons were valid (i.e. 1,1,1), all month polygons
invalid (i.e. 0,0,0), and one of the three number polygons valid
(0,1,0), the participant’s score would be 4/9 ≈ 0.44.

#### Compactness Score

We evaluated polygon compactness with the Polsby-Popper score
[@polsby1991], which was developed to quantify the compactness of
electoral districts, e.g., to detect gerrymandering. Gerrymandering is a
politically motivated strategy of redefining electoral districts’
borders to advantage a political party. Hence gerrymandered districts
should be less compact than districts that follow geomorphological
properties. Analogously, SSS forms originating from perceptual
experience may have topological properties that lead to more compact
forms compared to controls' responses.

The compactness score is calculated as the ratio of the polygon's area
to the area of a circle with the same perimeter. The score compares the
area enclosed by a polygon with its boundary length. Hence values near 1
indicate a compact, circle-like polygon, whereas values near 0 indicate
an elongated or irregular polygon. Formally, the Polsby-Popper score is
calculated from the polygon’s area and perimeter [@eq-PP]. For forms
with a perimeter of 0 (i.e. clicking on the same position), we
attributed a Polsby-Popper score of 0.

$$Polsby - Popper\ score = \frac{4\pi \cdot Area}{Perimeter^2}$$ {#eq-PP}

For example, a Polsby-Popper score of 1 represents maximal compactness,
i.e. overlapping to a perfect circle (see @fig-03 for an example of very
circular forms). Again, scores were averaged across the three categories
and three repetitions per participant, resulting in scores between 0 and
1, with higher values expected for synaesthetes.

### Permutation-based Feature Extraction {#sec-permutation-based-feature-extraction}

When constructing the segments and polygons, each form's ordinal
position is determined by the coordinates within each repetition (i.e. 0
(rep. 1) `→` 1 (rep. 1) `→` … `→` 9 (rep. 1); vs. 0 (rep. 2) `→` 1 (rep.
2) `→` … `→` 9 (rep. 2)). Hence, we also recalculated selected metrics
on forms re-created by permuting repetition labels across stimuli within
a category. This second analysis assessed whether form-level properties
were preserved when a form combined coordinates from different
repetitions. The rationale is that consistent spatial forms should have
the same geometrical properties independently from the repetition order.

We permuted the repetition labels assigned to each stimulus to create
permuted forms (@fig-01 D). For each permutation, the repetition label
was randomly shuffled across stimulus per participants, for example
Monday (repetition 2) `→` Tuesday (repetition 3) `→` Wednesday
(repetition 1) and so on. We then recalculated the form-level metrics.

We applied this procedure to the two form-level metrics with the
strongest initial discrimination: topological validity and Polsby-Popper
compactness. This procedure was repeated 500 times for each participant,
and the permuted values were then averaged to obtain a single
permutation score per participant.

### Receiver Operating Characteristic Analyses {#sec-receiver-operating-characteristic-analyses}

Each metric was evaluated against self-reported synaesthetes and
controls. The hypothesised direction of each metric was fixed before the
ROC analyses: smaller triangle areas and perimeters, smaller polygon
perimeters and fewer self-intersections were expected for synaesthetes,
as were larger polygon areas and higher simplicity, validity and
Polsby-Popper scores. ROC curves summarise discrimination across all
possible metrics' cutoffs. Classification performance was quantified
using the AUC with DeLong 95% confidence intervals [@delong1988],
cutoffs were selected with Youden’s index [@youden1950] from which the
corresponding sensitivity and specificity were calculated.
Discrimination power (DP; @eq-DP) provided an additional summary at the
selected cutoff; values below 1 indicate poor discrimination. DP could
not be computed when sensitivity or specificity was 100%.

$$ 
DP = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{\pi} (\log(\frac{sensitivity}{1−sensitivity}) + \log(\frac{specificity}{1−specificity}))  $$ {#eq-DP}

We compared paired AUCs using a bootstrapping method with 1000
re-samples, since this method allows comparing metrics with different
directions. *D* is the difference between the two AUCs divided by the
standard deviation of the bootstrap differences (@eq-D).

$$D = \frac{AUC_1-AUC_2}{SD}$$ {#eq-D}

Each metric was compared with the metric that led to the highest AUC.
*p*-values were adjusted using the false discovery rate (FDR) procedure
[@benjamini1995] over all paired comparisons.

```{r, triangleArea_fun}
# Define area calculation function
triangle_area <- function(x, y) {
  if(length(x) != 3 | length(y) != 3) return(NA)
  area <- abs(
    x[1]*y[2] + x[2]*y[3] + x[3]*y[1] -
    x[1]*y[3] - x[2]*y[1] - x[3]*y[2]
  ) / 2
  return(area)
}
```

```{r, area_Consitency}
## Triangle area per stimulus:
ds <- ds %>%  
  group_by(ID, stimulus) %>%
  mutate(rep_area = triangle_area(x, y)) %>%
  ungroup()

## Merge
tmp_perID2 <- ds %>% 
    ungroup() %>% 
    group_by(ID) %>% 
    reframe(Area_perc = sum(rep_area, na.rm = TRUE)/(sum(!is.na(rep_area)))*100, Screen_area = unique(Screen_area))  %>%
  select(ID, Area_perc,Screen_area)

tmp_perID2$Area_perc <- tmp_perID2$Area_perc/tmp_perID2$Screen_area
tmp_perID2 <- tmp_perID2 %>% select(ID, Area_perc)
ds_Q <- merge(ds_Q,tmp_perID2,by = "ID")

feature_direction <- c("moreCtl")
rm(tmp_perID2)
```

```{r, area_zsConsitency}
## Same with z-scores:
ds <- ds %>%  
  group_by(ID, stimulus) %>%
  mutate(rep_area_zs = triangle_area(x_zs, y_zs)) %>%
  ungroup()

## Merge
tmp_perID2 <- ds %>% ungroup() %>% 
  group_by(ID) %>% 
  reframe(Area_zs = mean(rep_area_zs, na.rm = TRUE))  %>%
  select(ID, Area_zs)

ds_Q <- merge(ds_Q,tmp_perID2,by = "ID")
rm(tmp_perID2)

feature_direction <- c(feature_direction,"moreCtl")
```

```{r, perimFun}
### Perimeter function: 
triangle_perimeter <- function(x, y) {
  if(length(x) != 3 | length(y) != 3) return(NA)
  # Side lengths
  a <- sqrt((x[2] - x[1])^2 + (y[2] - y[1])^2)
  b <- sqrt((x[3] - x[2])^2 + (y[3] - y[2])^2)
  c <- sqrt((x[1] - x[3])^2 + (y[1] - y[3])^2)
  perimeter <- a + b + c
  return(perimeter)
}
```

```{r, selfInter_fun}

# Define function:
count_self_intersections <- function(x, y, verbose = TRUE) {
  n <- length(x)
  if (n < 4) {
    if (verbose) cat("Need at least 4 points to check for self-intersection.\n")
    return(0)
  }

  # Orientation function
  orientation <- function(p, q, r) {
    val <- (q[2] - p[2]) * (r[1] - q[1]) - (q[1] - p[1]) * (r[2] - q[2])
    if (is.na(val)) return(NA)
    if (val == 0) return(0)
    if (val > 0) return(1) else return(2)
  }

  # Check if q lies on segment pr
  on_segment <- function(p, q, r) {
    if (any(is.na(c(p, q, r)))) return(FALSE)
    q[1] <= max(p[1], r[1]) && q[1] >= min(p[1], r[1]) &&
      q[2] <= max(p[2], r[2]) && q[2] >= min(p[2], r[2])
  }

  # Main intersection check
  segments_intersect <- function(p1, p2, p3, p4) {
    o1 <- orientation(p1, p2, p3)
    o2 <- orientation(p1, p2, p4)
    o3 <- orientation(p3, p4, p1)
    o4 <- orientation(p3, p4, p2)

    if (any(is.na(c(o1, o2, o3, o4)))) return(FALSE)

    # General case
    if (o1 != o2 && o3 != o4) return(TRUE)

    # Special colinear cases
    if (o1 == 0 && on_segment(p1, p3, p2)) return(TRUE)
    if (o2 == 0 && on_segment(p1, p4, p2)) return(TRUE)
    if (o3 == 0 && on_segment(p3, p1, p4)) return(TRUE)
    if (o4 == 0 && on_segment(p3, p2, p4)) return(TRUE)

    return(FALSE)
  }

  count <- 0
  for (i in 1:(n - 2)) {
    for (j in (i + 2):(n - 1)) {
      if (j == i + 1) next  # skip adjacent segments

      p1 <- c(x[i], y[i])
      p2 <- c(x[i + 1], y[i + 1])
      p3 <- c(x[j], y[j])
      p4 <- c(x[j + 1], y[j + 1])

      if (segments_intersect(p1, p2, p3, p4)) {
        count <- count + 1
        if (verbose) {
          cat(sprintf("Intersection #%d: segments (%d-%d) and (%d-%d)\n", count, i, i+1, j, j+1))
        }
      }
    }
  }

  if (verbose) cat("Total crossings:", count, "\n")
  return(count)
}

```

```{r permuteAcrossRep}
#| include: false

# Permutation of the repetition labels across stimuli (see Methods, Permutation-based Feature Extraction).
# For each participant and stimulus, the three repetition labels are shuffled. Permuted forms are rebuilt
# as polygons; topological validity and the Polsby-Popper score are averaged over ALL forms (up to 9:
# 3 categories x 3 repetitions) of the participant. This is repeated n_perms times.
# Vectorised re-implementation of the MS7 loop: with the identity permutation it reproduces
# isValidStruct_M and pp_M exactly. Results are saved and only recomputed if the files are missing (~2 min).

perm_file_valid <- "Data/permuted_isValid_MS8.csv"
perm_file_pp    <- "Data/permuted_pp_MS8.csv"
n_perms         <- 500

if(!file.exists(perm_file_valid) | !file.exists(perm_file_pp)){
  sf::sf_use_s2(FALSE)
  stim_levels <- c(as.character(0:9),
                   "Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday", "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday",
                   "January", "February", "March", "April", "May", "June", "July", "August",
                   "September", "October", "November", "December")

  d_perm <- ds %>%
    ungroup() %>%
    select(ID, Cond, stimulus, repetition, x_zs, y_zs) %>%
    mutate(ID = as.character(ID), x_zs = as.numeric(x_zs), y_zs = as.numeric(y_zs),
           StimOrder = match(stimulus, stim_levels)) %>%
    arrange(ID, Cond, StimOrder, repetition)

  # One element per ID x Cond with [n stimuli x 3 repetitions] coordinate matrices (ordinal order kept)
  forms <- lapply(split(d_perm, list(d_perm$ID, d_perm$Cond), drop = TRUE), function(g){
    stopifnot(nrow(g) %% 3 == 0) # each stimulus has exactly 3 repetitions (see FilterTrials)
    n_stim <- nrow(g)/3
    list(ID = g$ID[1],
         X  = matrix(g$x_zs, n_stim, 3, byrow = TRUE),
         Y  = matrix(g$y_zs, n_stim, 3, byrow = TRUE))
  })

  # Build all permuted polygons of one permutation and compute validity and Polsby-Popper score
  permute_once <- function(forms){
    geoms <- vector("list", length(forms)*3)
    ids   <- character(length(forms)*3)
    k <- 0
    for(f in forms){
      n_stim <- nrow(f$X)
      P <- t(replicate(n_stim, sample(3))) # new repetition label of each stimulus
      for(r in 1:3){
        k <- k + 1
        idx <- cbind(1:n_stim, P[, r])
        geoms[[k]] <- st_linestring(cbind(f$X[idx], f$Y[idx]))
        ids[k] <- f$ID
      }
    }
    polys <- st_cast(st_sfc(geoms), "POLYGON")
    area  <- as.numeric(st_area(polys))
    perim <- as.numeric(st_length(st_boundary(polys)))
    pp    <- (4 * pi * area) / (perim^2)
    pp[is.na(pp)] <- 0 # perimeter of 0: pp = 0, as for the non-permuted pp_M
    data.frame(ID = ids,
               valid = st_is_valid(polys, geos_method = "valid_structure"),
               pp = pp) %>%
      group_by(ID) %>%
      summarise(valid = mean(valid, na.rm = TRUE), pp = mean(pp, na.rm = TRUE))
  }

  set.seed(42)
  ID_list    <- unique(d_perm$ID)
  perm_names <- paste0("n_perm", sprintf("%03d", 1:n_perms))
  M_valid <- matrix(NA_real_, length(ID_list), n_perms, dimnames = list(ID_list, perm_names))
  M_pp    <- M_valid
  for(Perm_n in 1:n_perms){
    res <- permute_once(forms)
    M_valid[res$ID, Perm_n] <- res$valid
    M_pp[res$ID, Perm_n]    <- res$pp
  }

  write.csv2(data.frame(M_valid, ID = ID_list), perm_file_valid, row.names = FALSE)
  write.csv2(data.frame(M_pp,    ID = ID_list), perm_file_pp,    row.names = FALSE)
  rm(d_perm, forms, permute_once, M_valid, M_pp, res, ID_list, perm_names, stim_levels)
}
```

# Results - Phase I {#sec-results}

```{r, defineDPfun}
DP <- function(sensitivity, specificity){
  # Discrimination power (eq-DP)
  sensitivity = sensitivity/100
  specificity = specificity/100
  dp <- (sqrt(3)/pi)*(log(sensitivity/(1-sensitivity)) + log(specificity/(1-specificity)))
  # DP is not computable when sensitivity or specificity is 0% or 100%:
  dp[!is.finite(dp)] <- NA
  return(dp)
}
```

```{r, InitializeROC_fun}
## Define function to compute ROC:
Comp_ROC <- function(data, group_col, feature, ID, Ord){
  # Ord: must be: moreSyn or moreCtl. Whether feature values are higher in Syn or Ctl.
  if(!setequal(levels(data[[group_col]]), c("Syn","Ctl"))){
    return(warning("group name must include: Syn Ctl"))
  }
  
  if (Ord == "moreSyn") {
    Dirhere <- "<"
  } else if (Ord == "moreCtl") {
    Dirhere <- ">"
  } else {
    return(warning("Ord must be moreSyn or moreCtl"))  
  }
  
  ################ ROC analyses ################ 
  ROC_here <- pROC::roc(data[[group_col]] ~ data[[feature]], data,
                  direction= Dirhere,
                  percent=TRUE,
                  ci=TRUE # AUC 95% CI with the DeLong method (pROC default)
                  )
  
  # Best threshold using Youden's J
  best_coords <- pROC::coords(ROC_here, "best", 
                              ret = c("accuracy","threshold", "sensitivity","specificity","ppv","npv"), 
                              best.method = "youden")
  

  auc_val <- as.numeric(pROC::auc(ROC_here))
  ci_auc  <- ci.auc(ROC_here)
  ciobj   <- pROC::ci.se(ROC_here, # CI of sensitivity
               specificities=seq(0, 100, 5)) # over a select set of specificities

  new_row <- data.frame(
    Feature   = feature,
    AUC        = round(auc_val, 4),
    DP         = DP(as.numeric(best_coords[["sensitivity"]]),as.numeric(best_coords[["specificity"]])),
    threshold  = as.numeric(best_coords[["threshold"]]),
    sensitivity= as.numeric(best_coords[["sensitivity"]]),
    specificity= as.numeric(best_coords[["specificity"]]),
    ci_low     = as.numeric(ci_auc[1]),
    ci_high    = as.numeric(ci_auc[3]),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  
  ################ Contingency table ################ 
    if (Ord == "moreSyn") {
    data$diagnosis <- ifelse(data[[feature]] >= best_coords$threshold,  "Test : Syn", "Test : Ctl")
  } else if (Ord == "moreCtl") {
    data$diagnosis <- ifelse(data[[feature]] >= best_coords$threshold,  "Test : Ctl","Test : Syn")
  } else {
    warning("Ord must be moreSyn or moreCtl")  
  }
  
  tab_counts <- table(data[[group_col]], data$diagnosis)
  
  tab_percent <- prop.table(tab_counts, margin = 1) * 100
  
  result <- matrix(
    paste0(tab_counts, " (", round(tab_percent, 1), "%)"),
    nrow = nrow(tab_counts),
    dimnames = dimnames(tab_counts)
  )
  
  ################ General description ################ 
  # Attention, na removed  
  Descr_table <- data %>%
    group_by(!!sym(group_col)) %>%
    reframe(n = length(unique(!!sym(ID))), Mean = mean(!!sym(feature), na.rm = TRUE), SD = sd(!!sym(feature), na.rm = TRUE))

  ################ Return outputs ################ 
  return(list(ROC_properties = new_row, Coningency_table =result, Descr_table = Descr_table, ROC_curve = ROC_here, CI = ciobj))
}
```

```{r compROCallFeat}
# Features and their hypothesised direction are matched by NAME, not by column position.

                             isSimple_GA     = "moreSyn",
                             isValidStruct_M = "moreSyn",
                             isValid_perm_M  = "moreSyn",
                             pp_M            = "moreSyn",
                             pp_perm_M       = "moreSyn")

# Sanity checks: every feature exists, and the directions appended chunk-by-chunk above agree.
stopifnot(all(names(feature_direction_named) %in% colnames(ds_Q)))
stopifnot(identical(unname(feature_direction_named), feature_direction))

feature_list      <- names(feature_direction_named)
feature_direction <- unname(feature_direction_named)
Feats <- as.matrix(t(rbind(feature_list,feature_direction)))

# Now we will loop through features: INITIALIZE ROC_curves
ROC_curves <- list()

# Initialize dataframe to collect relevant ROC values:
All_ROC <- data.frame(Feature=character(),
                      AUC         = character(),
                      threshold   = integer(),
                      sensitivity = integer(),
                      specificity = integer(),
                      ppv         = integer(),
                      npv         = integer(),
                      high_ci     = integer(),
                      low_ci      = integer(),
                      stringsAsFactors=FALSE)

# Loop by features:
for(fit_n in 1:length(Feats[,1])){
  ROC_here <- Comp_ROC(ds_Q, "group", Feats[[fit_n,1]],"ID", Feats[[fit_n,2]])
  
  ROC_curves      <- c(ROC_curves,list(ROC_here$ROC_curve,ROC_here$ROC_properties$Feature))
  All_ROC         <- rbind(All_ROC, ROC_here$ROC_properties)
}
```

```{r, AUCtest}
# Since random sampling is involved in bootstrapping, to make it reproducible:
set.seed(42)

# Compare ALL the features and adjust, but leads to the same results.
nFeat    <- length(ROC_curves)
Odd_idx  <- seq(1,nFeat,by=2)
Pair_idx <- seq(2,nFeat,by=2)

ROC_listed <- list()
Feattype <- c()
for(i in 1:nFeat){
  ROC_listed[[i]] <- ROC_curves[[Odd_idx[i]]]
  Feattype <- c(Feattype,ROC_curves[[Pair_idx[i]]])
}

allAUC  <- sapply(ROC_listed, auc)
sel_auc <- which(allAUC == sort(allAUC, decreasing = TRUE)[1])
toCompare_roc <- ROC_listed[[sel_auc]] 

# Run roc.test() once per pair, so that D and p come from the same bootstrap:
ROC_tests <- lapply(seq_along(ROC_listed), function(i) {
  if (i == sel_auc) return(NULL)
  roc.test(toCompare_roc, ROC_listed[[i]],  boot.n=1000,method = "bootstrap", paired = TRUE)
})
statistic <- sapply(ROC_tests, function(t) if (is.null(t)) NA else unname(t$statistic))
pvals     <- sapply(ROC_tests, function(t) if (is.null(t)) NA else t$p.value)

# Adjust for multiple comparison: the order is Feattype
pvals_adj <- p.adjust(pvals, method = "fdr")

Results_ROCcomp <- data.frame(
  Feature = Feattype,
  D = statistic,
  pvals = pvals_adj,
  isSign = (pvals_adj <.05)
)
```

```{r, AUCdiffCI}
# AUC difference (best metric minus each other metric) with a 95% percentile bootstrap CI
# (1000 stratified resamples of participants). Non-significance does not show equivalence; the CI
# shows which differences remain compatible with the data.
set.seed(42)
n_boot   <- 1000
best_feat <- Feattype[sel_auc]
idx_syn  <- which(ds_Q$group == "Syn")
idx_ctl  <- which(ds_Q$group == "Ctl")
auc_fast <- function(data, f){
  as.numeric(pROC::auc(pROC::roc(data$group, data[[f]], levels = c("Ctl","Syn"),
                                 direction = ifelse(feature_direction_named[[f]] == "moreSyn", "<", ">"),
                                 percent = TRUE, quiet = TRUE)))
}
boot_diff <- replicate(n_boot, {
  b <- ds_Q[c(sample(idx_syn, replace = TRUE), sample(idx_ctl, replace = TRUE)), ]
  a_best <- auc_fast(b, best_feat)
  sapply(feature_list, function(f) a_best - auc_fast(b, f))
})
AUC_diff <- data.frame(
  Feature = feature_list,
  diff    = sapply(feature_list, function(f) auc_fast(ds_Q, best_feat) - auc_fast(ds_Q, f)),
  ci_low  = apply(boot_diff, 1, quantile, 0.025),
  ci_high = apply(boot_diff, 1, quantile, 0.975)
)
rm(boot_diff)
```

```{r, OperatingPointTests}
# Exploratory comparisons at fixed operating points (not pre-specified):
# Polsby-Popper compactness vs standardised perimeter, sensitivity at 80% specificity and
# specificity at 80% sensitivity (paired bootstrap, 1000 resamples), FDR-adjusted within this family.
set.seed(42)
roc_pp    <- ROC_listed[[which(Feattype == "pp_M")]]
roc_perim <- ROC_listed[[which(Feattype == "Perimeter_zs")]]
OP_tests <- list(
  sens_at_spec80 = roc.test(roc_pp, roc_perim, method = "specificity", specificity = 80,
                            boot.n = 1000, paired = TRUE),
  spec_at_sens80 = roc.test(roc_pp, roc_perim, method = "sensitivity", sensitivity = 80,
                            boot.n = 1000, paired = TRUE)
)
OP_res <- data.frame(
  test  = names(OP_tests),
  D     = sapply(OP_tests, function(t) unname(t$statistic)),
  p     = sapply(OP_tests, function(t) t$p.value)
)
OP_res$p_adj <- p.adjust(OP_res$p, method = "fdr")
# Sensitivity (at 80% specificity) and specificity (at 80% sensitivity) of each metric:
OP_values <- data.frame(
  metric         = c("pp_M", "Perimeter_zs"),
  sens_at_spec80 = c(as.numeric(coords(roc_pp, 80, input = "specificity", ret = "sensitivity")),
                     as.numeric(coords(roc_perim, 80, input = "specificity", ret = "sensitivity"))),
  spec_at_sens80 = c(as.numeric(coords(roc_pp, 80, input = "sensitivity", ret = "specificity")),
                     as.numeric(coords(roc_perim, 80, input = "sensitivity", ret = "specificity")))
)

# Inline-reporting helpers
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(p < .001, "< .001", paste0("= ", sub("^0", "", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = 3))))
fmt_D <- function(f) formatC(Results_ROCcomp$D[Results_ROCcomp$Feature == f], format = "f", digits = 2)
fmt_pD <- function(f) fmt_p(Results_ROCcomp$pvals[Results_ROCcomp$Feature == f])
fmt_auc <- function(f) formatC(All_ROC$AUC[All_ROC$Feature == f], format = "f", digits = 2)
fmt_ci  <- function(f) paste0("[", formatC(All_ROC$ci_low[All_ROC$Feature == f], format = "f", digits = 2), "%, ",
                             formatC(All_ROC$ci_high[All_ROC$Feature == f], format = "f", digits = 2), "%]")
fmt_diff <- function(f) {r <- AUC_diff[AUC_diff$Feature == f, ]
  paste0(formatC(r$diff, format = "f", digits = 2), " percentage points, 95% CI [",
         formatC(r$ci_low, format = "f", digits = 2), ", ", formatC(r$ci_high, format = "f", digits = 2), "]")}
```

## Descriptive Results of Reproduced Metrics

Among self-reported SSS participants, mean triangle area of the
aggregated datasets was
`r round(mean(ds_Q$Area_perc[ds_Q$group == "Syn"]),2)`% of the screen
area (*SD* = `r round(sd(ds_Q$Area_perc[ds_Q$group == "Syn"]),2)`%),
compared with 0.14% (*SD* = 0.13%) in @rothen2016 and 0.14% (*SD* =
0.17%) in @ward2018. The value in @rothen2016 is reproduced when only
that dataset is used (see @apx-SM2byds). Per-dataset descriptives
suggest that the largest dataset, @ward2022a, contributed substantially
to the larger area (*M* =
`r round(mean(ds_Q$Area_perc[ds_Q$group == "Syn" & ds_Q$dataSource == "Ward"]),2)`%;
@tbl-apx02).

Overall, synaesthetes' mean triangle area in the pooled data was about

## ROC Analyses

Permuted topological validity had the highest AUC
(`r fmt_auc("isValid_perm_M")`%, 95% CI `r fmt_ci("isValid_perm_M")`),
followed by Polsby-Popper compactness (`r fmt_auc("pp_M")`%, 95% CI
`r fmt_ci("pp_M")`) and standardised within-stimulus perimeter
(`r fmt_auc("Perimeter_zs")`%, 95% CI `r fmt_ci("Perimeter_zs")`). After
FDR correction, neither Polsby-Popper compactness (*D* =
`r fmt_D("pp_M")`, *p* `r fmt_pD("pp_M")`) nor standardised perimeter
(*D* = `r fmt_D("Perimeter_zs")`, *p* `r fmt_pD("Perimeter_zs")`)
differed significantly from permuted validity. All other metrics had
significantly lower AUCs. @tbl-03 and @fig-05 summarise the ROC results
by descending AUC. @fig-apx01 shows the group distributions for all
metrics. Discrimination power was limited for all metrics (DP ≤
`r formatC(max(All_ROC$DP, na.rm = TRUE), format = "f", digits = 2)`).

```{r}
#| label: fig-05
#| fig-cap: "Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curves of all consistency metrics"
#| apa-note: "The diagonal grey line represents chance-level discrimination. Curves are oriented so that movement toward the upper-left corner indicates better performance."

nFeat <- length(ROC_curves)
Odd_idx  <- seq(1,nFeat,by=2)
Pair_idx <- seq(2,nFeat,by=2)

ROC_listed <- list()
Feattype <- c()
for(i in 1:nFeat){
  ROC_listed[[i]] <- ROC_curves[[Odd_idx[i]]]
  Feattype <- c(Feattype,ROC_curves[[Pair_idx[i]]])
}

Feattype <- recode(Feattype, 
                   "Area_perc" = "Area [screen size %]",
                   "Area_zs" =  "Area [z-score]", 
                   "Perimeter_perc" = "Perimeter [screen size %]",
                   "Perimeter_zs" = "Perimeter [z-score]",
                   "SelfInter" = "Segment self-intersections [n/9]",
                   "areaPoly_GA" = "Area of the polygon [z-score]",
                   "perimPoly" = "Perimeter of the polygon [z-score]" ,   
                   "isSimple_GA" = "Simple topology [boolean/9]",
                   "isValidStruct_M" = "Valid structure [boolean/9]",
                   "isValid_perm_M" = "Permuted valid structure [boolean/9]",
                   "pp_M" = "Polsby-Popper [score/9]",
                   "pp_perm_M" = "Permuted P-P [score/9]"
                  )

# Arrows point at the Youden cutoff of each metric (x = specificity, y = sensitivity):
op_pt <- function(f) c(All_ROC$specificity[All_ROC$Feature == f], All_ROC$sensitivity[All_ROC$Feature == f])

ggroc(ROC_listed) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = 100, y = 100, yend = 0),
               color="grey", size = 0.01) +
  scale_color_manual(labels = Feattype,values =pals::cols25(nFeat/2)) + # pals::brewer.pastel1(nFeat)
  papaja::theme_apa()+

           curvature = .3, arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), color = "#b2df8a", alpha = 0.5) +

  annotate(geom = "curve", x = op_pt("pp_M")[1], y = op_pt("pp_M")[2], xend = 33, yend = 60, 
           curvature = .3, arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), color = "#CAB2D6", alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = 33, y = 60, label = "Polsby-Popper", 
           hjust = "left", color = "#CAB2D6", size = 3) +
  
  
  annotate(geom = "curve", x = op_pt("Perimeter_zs")[1], y = op_pt("Perimeter_zs")[2], xend = 42, yend = 51, 
           curvature = -.3, arrow = arrow(length = unit(2, "mm")), color = "#6A33C2" , alpha = 0.5) +
  annotate(geom = "text", x = 42, y = 51, label = "Perimeter", 
           hjust = "left", color = "#6A33C2" , size = 3)
```

```{r}
  gt() %>%

  tab_footnote(footnote = "Note: AUC = area under the curve; CI = DeLong confidence interval; DP = discrimination power (n.c. = not computable because sensitivity or specificity was 100%). AUC, sensitivity and specificity are percentages. Cutoffs were selected with Youden’s index.") %>%
    tab_options( footnotes.multiline = TRUE)
```

Youden’s index identified a cutoff of
`r formatC(All_ROC[All_ROC$Feature == "isValid_perm_M",]$threshold, format = "f", digits = 2)`
for permuted validity, which corresponds to an average of
`r round(All_ROC[All_ROC$Feature == "isValid_perm_M",]$threshold*9, 1)`
valid forms out of 9. For standardised perimeter, scores below
`r round(All_ROC[All_ROC$Feature == "Perimeter_zs",]$threshold,2)` were
classified as SSS-like. For Polsby-Popper compactness, scores above
`r round(All_ROC[All_ROC$Feature == "pp_M",]$threshold,2)` were
classified as SSS-like.

To further test the stability of these results, we conducted additional
analyses across the different datasets and with different
questionnaire-based grouping. Several metrics had comparably high AUCs,
but their ranking order differed across datasets (see @fig-apx02).

```{r, AdditionalInline}
# Values reported in the Additional Analyses text, computed here so that the text is not hard-coded.
# Same rules as the appendix chunks (full-sample cutoffs,
# hypothesised direction of each metric).
top5 <- All_ROC$Feature[order(All_ROC$AUC, decreasing = TRUE)][1:5]

class_syn <- sapply(top5, function(f){
  th <- All_ROC$threshold[All_ROC$Feature == f]
  if (feature_direction_named[[f]] == "moreSyn") ds_Q[[f]] >= th else ds_Q[[f]] <= th
})
keep_alluvial <- ds_Q$ID != "69253" # as in the alluvial appendix figure
n_consFN <- sum(ds_Q$group == "Syn" & rowSums(class_syn) == 0 & keep_alluvial)
n_consFP <- sum(ds_Q$group == "Ctl" & rowSums(class_syn) == 5 & keep_alluvial)
pct_N    <- function(n) formatC(100 * n / nrow(ds_Q), format = "f", digits = 0)

# Correlations with the questionnaire score (Ward datasets only).
# Higher questionnaire scores indicate weaker self-reported SSS.
ds_Qw <- ds_Q %>% filter(!is.na(`questionnaire score`))
cor_q <- lapply(top5, function(f) cor.test(ds_Qw$`questionnaire score`, ds_Qw[[f]]))
names(cor_q) <- top5
fmt_r <- function(f) paste0("*r* = ", sub("0\\.", ".", formatC(cor_q[[f]]$estimate, format = "f", digits = 2)),
                            ", *p* ", fmt_p(cor_q[[f]]$p.value))
```

## Additional Analyses

Additional analyses addressed four questions. First, we examined whether
the metrics led to stable results across datasets and questionnaire
scores. Second, we examined the correlations between consistency metrics
and questionnaire scores. Third, we examined which spatial forms led to
false negatives (self-reported synaesthetes' forms classified as
controls) and false positives (self-reported controls' forms classified
as synaesthetes) for each metric. Fourth, we checked for participants
who were consistently classified as the other group across metrics.

First, for the metrics with an AUC of at least 75%, we recalculated AUC,
sensitivity, and specificity for each dataset. Both the rank ordering
and the performance estimates varied across data sources (@fig-apx02).
For example, standardised perimeter had the highest AUC in the
@ward2022a dataset but the lowest of the five leading metrics in the
@vanpetersen2020 dataset. @fig-apx03 shows substantial overlap between
the groups' distributions within several datasets. Using the data from
the Ward datasets, which also contain the individual questionnaire
responses, we compared progressively broader score groups depending on
questionnaire responses: the lowest and highest 10%, then the lowest and
highest 20%, and so forth, up to the whole Ward sample (lowest and
highest 50%). Absolute performance was strongest for the most extreme
questionnaire-based groups and declined as the sampled groups became
less distinct, although the relative ordering of the leading metrics was
generally stable (@fig-apx04).

Second, we examined correlations between questionnaire scores and the
five leading metrics in the Ward datasets. A concern is criterion
circularity when consistency scores contribute to the original group
labels [@root2025]. The strongest correlations were observed for
standardised perimeter (`r fmt_r("Perimeter_zs")`) and permuted validity
(`r fmt_r("isValid_perm_M")`; @fig-apx05). In both cases, more
consistent responses went with stronger self-reported SSS.

Third, we visually inspected false negatives (@fig-apx10) and positives
(@fig-apx11) across permuted validity, standardised perimeter and
Polsby-Popper scores. Among false negatives, several curved forms by
self-reported synaesthetes were incorrectly classified as controls with
the standardised perimeter metric; linear forms with the Polsby-Popper
metric. Among false positives, the permuted validity metric
misclassified controls' forms arranged approximately horizontally, and
the Polsby-Popper metric misclassified irregular, zigzag forms. The
perimeter metric misclassified highly linear forms, or forms in which
the participant clicked in approximately the same position repeatedly,
as synaesthetic.

Fourth, some participants may have been misclassified in the
self-report, and some may represent consistent controls or inconsistent
synaesthetes [@root2025; @eagleman2007]. Across the five leading
metrics, `r n_consFN` self-reported SSS participants (approximately
`r pct_N(n_consFN)`% of the full sample) were consistently classified as
controls (i.e. consistent false negatives; @fig-apx08), whereas
`r n_consFP` controls (approximately `r pct_N(n_consFP)`%) were
consistently classified as SSS (i.e. consistent false positives;
@fig-apx09).

In sum, metrics' classification performance varied across datasets and
decreased as questionnaire-based groups became less extreme. Visual
inspections suggested that while stimulus-level metrics such as
perimeter tend to classify synaesthetic curved forms as control,
form-level metrics such as topological validity and Polsby-Popper score
tend to classify horizontally arranged forms from controls as
synaesthetes. In total, `r n_consFN + n_consFP` participants (about
`r pct_N(n_consFN + n_consFP)`%) were misclassified by all five leading
metrics.

# Methods - Phase II {#sec-phase-ii-methods}

Phase II will test whether the five metrics with an AUC of at least 75%
lead to comparable AUC scores and cutoffs in an independent dataset. The
five selected metrics are: permuted validity, Polsby-Popper compactness,
standardised perimeter, topological validity and permuted Polsby-Popper.
This independent dataset will be collected as part of @sachdeva2024,
which received Stage 1 in-principle acceptance. The task will follow the
same methodology, besides that there will be four repetitions of each
stimuli instead of three. The confirmatory analysis will apply
prespecified metric definitions, classification directions, and cutoffs
from Phase I without re-optimisation. The Phase II protocol will also
specify how four response coordinates are combined for the
stimulus-level area and perimeter metrics. Sample size, recruitment, and
the full analysis plan are preregistered at <https://osf.io/6wn4m>.

# Discussion - Phase I

Across four datasets, form-level permuted topological validity,
Polsby-Popper compactness and stimulus-level standardised perimeter
provided the strongest discrimination between self-reported SSS
participants and controls. Their AUCs did not differ significantly. This
suggests that our form-level descriptor performs comparably to an
established stimulus-level consistency metric. Performance, however,
varied across datasets. This heterogeneity may explain why triangle
area, the strongest metric in @rothen2016, performed worse in the
aggregated sample than expected. In the Ward datasets, the relative
ranking of the metrics with AUCs of at least 75% remained similar across
questionnaire-score subsamples, although absolute performance decreased
as less extreme groups were included. Standardised perimeter also
correlated slightly more strongly with questionnaire scores than
permuted validity.

In sum, the novel form-level permuted validity performed comparably to
the stimulus-level perimeter method. The two metrics capture different
aspects of the response pattern and may help identify different failure
modes. These results need validation in an independent sample (Phase
II).

## Limitations {#sec-limitations}

First, as shown in @fig-apx02, we found that the optimal criteria can
vary across datasets. These differences might be explained by different
sampling methods. For example, @vanpetersen2020 recruited SSS from over
one hundred candidates to maximise participant reporting synaesthetic
experiences.

Second, consistency tests contain only a limited set of sequential
stimuli (weekdays, months, and the digits 0-9). Some individuals may
experience SSS for other ordinal categories such as clock time,
temperature, or musical keys. The restricted number range may also miss
transitions at decades or hundreds that are prominent in some number
forms [@galton1880].

Third, diagnostic cutoffs assume categorical distinctions between
groups, but SSS may vary continuously [@price2013]. This limitation is
related to the circularity mentioned previously: diagnostic cutoffs as
calculated here depend on how SSS and controls are classified in the
first place [@simner2012]. External validity of the consistency test of
synaesthesia should therefore be examined, for example automaticity or
visual Gabor detection might be necessary to establish external validity
[@ward2018]. Indeed, definitional choices contribute to the wide range
of reported prevalence 4.4% [@brang2013], 8.1% [@ward2018], and 14%
[@seron1992].

## Interpretation of Topological Validity

Permuted topological validity led to comparable results to perimeter,
suggesting that SSS spatial forms may follow topological rules. This
result might in itself be informative about how SSS forms are mapped in
space. Indeed, spatial forms may follow topological rules analogous to
geographical and geometry-based space structures. Analogies between maps
and neuroscience have a long history (e.g., retinotopy, tonotopy or
somatotopy, see @eagleman2009). Therefore spatial forms might originate
from the mapping of ordinal or sequential stimuli onto idiosyncratic
visuo-spatial abilities following topological rules.

## Intermediary Conclusion {#sec-conclusions}

Phase I compared established stimulus-level consistency metrics with
novel form-level geometric tests. Permuted topological validity,
Polsby-Popper compactness and standardised within-stimulus perimeter led
to the best classification performance. Permuted topological validity
classified as well as conventional metrics. Its added value is mainly
theoretical. Self-reported synaesthetes seem to produce more compact and
topologically valid structures than controls. Standardised perimeter, by
contrast, quantifies the distance between repeated responses to each
inducer.

Phase II will test external validity of these metrics on a yet to be
acquired dataset.

### Appendix

The additional analyses in this appendix address several concerns.
@apx-featDensity shows whether score distributions are bimodal.
@apx-SM2byds shows whether AUC, DP, sensitivity and specificity vary
across datasets.

To address circularity concerns that we might find methods that best
classify synaesthetes and controls only from the self-reported groups,
we used two additional approaches. First, we tested sub-samples based on
percentiles of the questionnaire score distribution (see
@apx-byquestperc). The rationale is that a good consistency test should
keep its relative ranking among metrics from strong to weaker SSS. To do
this, we re-sampled the SSS and controls based on their questionnaire
distribution by percentiles (i.e., comparing 10% highest questionnaire
scores vs. 10% lowest, then 20% vs. 20%, etc.). In addition, we
correlated the questionnaire scores with the different consistency
metrics, see @apx-correlation-with-self-report.

We also wanted to visually characterise whether certain patterns occur
more frequently for some categories than others (e.g. circular patterns
for months and linear for numbers). We wanted to visualise how each
participant is classified by each metric.

From this we found a group of synaesthetes who were consistently
classified as controls by different methods, as well as a group of
controls who were consistently classified as synaesthetes, see
@apx-alluvial.

Finally, we visualise false positives and negatives of the consistency
methods (see @apx-false-positive-and-negative-analysis).

The following R packages were used for the data visualisation in the
appendix:
`r pakret::pkrt_list("ggridges","cowplot","ggalluvial","corrplot")`

```{r}
#| label: fig-apx00

na.rm <- function(x){x <- x[!is.na(x)]}

ID_number <- na.rm(ds_Q_W$ID[ds_Q_W$`Q2_numbers (1=present, 0=absent)` == 1] )

ID_month  <- na.rm(ds_Q_W$ID[ds_Q_W$`Q2_months  (1=present, 0=absent)`== 1] )

x <- list(SSS = ID_group, Number = ID_number, Day = ID_days, Month =ID_month)
```

# ROC Analysis by Dataset {#apx-SM2byds}

for each dataset, see @fig-apx02 and @tbl-apx02. Descriptively, we also
looked at the distributions of each metric across SSS and controls
(@fig-apx03). Note that the unpublished Ward dataset has more
synaesthetes than controls (5:1 ratio). Note that some of the metrics
led to 100% specificity in the @vanpetersen2020 dataset.

```{r AUCbyDataSource}
dataSources <- unique(ds$dataSource)
AUC_ds <- vector("list", length(dataSources))


for(i in 1:length(dataSources)){
  
  ds_here <- ds_Q %>% filter(dataSource %in% dataSources[i])
  
  # INITIALIZE ROC_curves
  ROC_curves <- list()
  
  # Initialize dataframe to collect relevant ROC values:
  Per_ds_ROC <- data.frame(Feature=character(),
                        AUC = character(),
                        threshold=integer(),
                        sensitivity=integer(),
                        specificity=integer(),
                        ppv = integer(),
                        npv = integer(),
                        high_ci = integer(),
                        low_ci = integer(),
                        stringsAsFactors=FALSE)
  
  # Loop by features:
  for(fit_n in 1:length(Feats[,1])){
    ROC_here <- Comp_ROC(ds_here, "group", Feats[[fit_n,1]],"ID", Feats[[fit_n,2]])
    
    ROC_curves      <- c(ROC_curves,list(ROC_here$ROC_curve,ROC_here$ROC_properties$Feature))
    Per_ds_ROC      <- rbind(Per_ds_ROC, ROC_here$ROC_properties)
  }
  
  Per_ds_round <- Per_ds_ROC %>% 
    mutate_if(is.numeric, round,2)
  
  Per_ds_round <- Per_ds_round[order(Per_ds_round$AUC, decreasing = TRUE), ]
  
  
   AUC_ds[[i]] <- data.frame(
    Feature = Per_ds_round$Feature,
    AUC = Per_ds_round$AUC,
    DP =  Per_ds_round$DP,
    Sensitivity = Per_ds_round$sensitivity,
    Specificity = Per_ds_round$specificity,
    dataSource = dataSources[i],
    N = length(ds_here$ID)
  )
}
```

```{r}
ggplot(ds_Q_zs, aes(x = zs, y = Feature, fill = group, color  = group, point_color = group)) + 
  geom_density_ridges(alpha = 0.5, 
                      jittered_points = FALSE, 
                      position = position_points_jitter(width = 0.05, height = 0), 
                      scale = 1,
                      quantile_lines = TRUE, quantiles = c(0.2, 0.5, 0.8)) +
  xlim(-3, 3) +
  papaja::theme_apa() +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Sequence-Space Synaesthetes" = "steelblue",
                               "Controls" = "firebrick")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("Sequence-Space Synaesthetes" = "steelblue",
                               "Controls" = "firebrick")) +
  labs(y = "Method", x = "z-score") +
  facet_grid(~ dataSource) +
    theme(legend.position = "none",axis.text=element_text(size=9))
```

# ROC Analysis Sub-sampled Data by Questionnaire Quantiles (10% steps) {#apx-byquestperc}

We sub-sampled the Ward datasets by questionnaire score. We first
selected participants with the lowest 10% and the highest 10% of scores,
then the lowest and highest 20%, and so on up to 50% and 50% (i.e. the
whole sample with questionnaire data). Absolute AUC, sensitivity and
specificity are expected to decrease as less extreme groups are
included. A valid metric should, however, keep its ranking relative to
the other metrics across sub-samples, see @fig-apx04.

```{r}
#| label: PrepROCperQuant
ds_Q2 <- ds_Q %>% filter(dataSource %in% c("Ward","Ward2")) %>% filter(!is.na(`questionnaire score`))

p <- seq(0,1,0.10)
quant <- quantile(ds_Q2$`questionnaire score`, probs = p)
quant <- as.numeric(quant)

n_steps <- floor(length(quant)/2) # 5 steps: 10/90, 20/80, 30/70, 40/60, 50/50 (= all Ward participants)
AUC_perctils <- vector("list", n_steps)

# Separate object names inside the loop, so that the full-sample All_ROC / All_ROC_round are NOT
# overwritten by the last sub-sample.
for(quant_n in 1:n_steps){
  
  All_ROC_q <- data.frame()
  
  # Lowest (quant_n x 10)% vs highest (quant_n x 10)% questionnaire scores.
  # quant[1] is the 0% quantile, so the lower bound is quant[quant_n + 1].
  q_low  <- quant[quant_n + 1]
  q_high <- quant[length(quant) - quant_n]
  ds_Q2_quant_n <- ds_Q2 %>% 
  filter(`questionnaire score` <= q_low | `questionnaire score` >= q_high)
  
  # Loop by features:
  for(fit_n in 1:length(Feats[,1])){
    ROC_here  <- Comp_ROC(ds_Q2_quant_n, "group", Feats[[fit_n,1]],"ID",Feats[[fit_n,2]])
    All_ROC_q <- rbind(All_ROC_q, ROC_here$ROC_properties)
  }
  
  All_ROC_q_round <- All_ROC_q %>% 
    mutate_if(is.numeric, round,2)
  All_ROC_q_round <- All_ROC_q_round[order(All_ROC_q_round$AUC, decreasing = TRUE), ]
  
  AUC_perctils[[quant_n]] <- data.frame(
    Feature = All_ROC_q_round$Feature,
    AUC = All_ROC_q_round$AUC,
    DP = All_ROC_q_round$DP,
    Sensitivity = All_ROC_q_round$sensitivity,
    Specificity = All_ROC_q_round$specificity,
    Quant_min = q_low,
    Quant_max = q_high,
    N = nrow(ds_Q2_quant_n),
    quant_n = quant_n
  )
}

AUC_perctils <- do.call(rbind, AUC_perctils)

AUC_perctils$quant_n <- factor(AUC_perctils$quant_n, levels = 1:n_steps,
                               labels = c("10 & 90%", "20 & 80%", "30 & 70%", "40 & 60%", "50 & 50% (all)"))
rm(All_ROC_q, All_ROC_q_round)
# Top 5 metrics of the FULL sample (All_ROC is no longer overwritten above):
AUC_perctils <- AUC_perctils %>%
  filter(Feature %in%  All_ROC$Feature[order(All_ROC$AUC, decreasing = TRUE)][1:5]) %>%
  mutate(Feature = recode(Feature,
                             "Area_perc" = "Area [screen size %]",
                          "Area_zs" = "Area [z-score]", 
                          "Perimeter_perc" = "Perimeter [screen size %]",
                          "Perimeter_zs" = "Perimeter [z-score]",
                          "areaPoly_GA" = "Area of the polygon [z-score]",
                          "perimPoly" = "Perimeter of the polygon [z-score]" ,
                          "isSimple_GA" = "Simple topology [boolean/9]",
                          "SelfInter" = "Segment self-intersections [n/9]",
                          "isValidStruct_M" = "Valid structure [boolean/9]",
                          "isValid_perm_M" =  "Permuted valid structure [boolean/9]",
                          "pp_M" = "Polsby-Popper [score/9]",
                          "pp_perm_M" = "Permuted P-P [score/9]"))
  
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-apx04
#| fig-cap: "Line plots of AUC, DP, sensitivity and specificity by questionnaire percentile"
#| apa-note: "Each point is a sub-sample of the Ward datasets with the lowest and highest x% of questionnaire scores (50 & 50% = all participants with questionnaire data). AUC = area under the curve; DP = discrimination power."

gp_AUC <- ggplot(AUC_perctils, aes(x = quant_n, y = AUC, group = Feature, colour = Feature)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values =pals::cols25(nFeat)) +
  papaja::theme_apa() +
  xlab(' ') +
  ylim(50,100) +
  theme(legend.position="none",axis.text.x = element_blank())

  geom_path() +
  geom_point() +

  papaja::theme_apa() +
  xlab(' ') +
  ylim(0, NA) +
  theme(legend.position="none",axis.text.x = element_blank())

gp_Sensitivity <- ggplot(AUC_perctils, aes(x = quant_n, y = Sensitivity, group = Feature, colour = Feature)) +
  geom_path() +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values =pals::cols25(nFeat)) +
  papaja::theme_apa() +
  xlab(' ') +
  ylim(50,100) +
  theme(legend.position="none",axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))

gp_Specificity <- ggplot(AUC_perctils, aes(x = quant_n, y = Specificity, group = Feature, colour = Feature)) +
  geom_path() +

  scale_color_manual(values =pals::cols25(nFeat)) +
  papaja::theme_apa() +
  xlab(' ') +
  ylim(50,100) +
  theme(legend.position="none",axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))


legend <- get_legend(
  ggplot(AUC_perctils, aes(x = quant_n, y = Specificity, group = Feature, colour = Feature)) +
    geom_point() +

     guides(color = guide_legend(nrow = 2)) +

           legend.text=ggplot2::element_text(size=10))
)


plot_grid(gp_AUC, gp_DP,gp_Sensitivity,gp_Specificity, 
          labels = c("A","B","C","D"),legend = legend, ncol=2,
```

# Correlation with Self-Report {#apx-correlation-with-self-report}

The best criterion should also correlate with questionnaire scores. This
was possible only for the Ward datasets, see @fig-apx05. Higher
questionnaire scores indicate weaker self-reported SSS.

```{r}
#| label: fig-apx05
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| apa-note: Only data from the two Ward datasets are included. Values are signed Pearson correlations; non-significant correlations (p ≥ .05) are left blank. Higher questionnaire scores indicate weaker self-reported SSS.
#| fig-cap: Correlation with self-reported questionnaire
#| fig-height: 9
#| fig-width: 9

sel_dsQ <- ds_Q %>%
  select(c(`questionnaire score`,feature_list)) %>%
  filter(!is.na(`questionnaire score`))  %>%
  select_if(~ !any(is.na(.)))

sel_dsQ <- sel_dsQ %>% 
  select(c("questionnaire score", all_of(top5))) %>% # full-sample top 5
  rename("Perimeter [standardised coordinates]" = "Perimeter_zs",
         "Valid structure [proportion of forms]" = "isValidStruct_M",
         "Permuted valid structure [proportion of forms]" = "isValid_perm_M",
         "Polsby-Popper [mean across forms]" = "pp_M",
          "Permuted Polsby-Popper [mean across forms]" = "pp_perm_M")

sel_CorMat <- cor(sel_dsQ)
sel_CorMat_test <- cor.mtest(sel_dsQ)
  

# Signed correlations. Higher questionnaire scores indicate weaker SSS self-report.
corrplot(sel_CorMat, method = 'number', diag=FALSE, type = "lower",tl.col = 'black', cl.pos = 'n',col = c('black', 'black'),
         p.mat = sel_CorMat_test$p, sig.level = .05, insig = "blank")
```

# False Positive and Negative Analysis {#apx-false-positive-and-negative-analysis}

To inspect patterns in false negatives (synaesthetes classified as
controls) and false positives (controls classified as synaesthetes), we
plotted false positives and negatives for permuted validity,
standardised perimeter and Polsby-Popper score, after applying the
respective cutoff. For each metric we only represent participants that
are uniquely flagged as false negatives or positives. For example, if a
participant is flagged as a false negative by permuted validity and
standardised perimeter, they are not shown here.

```{r}
#| label: PassorNot

ds_Q$pass_SynGroup <- ds_Q$group == "Syn" # True if self-report as syn

All_ROC_round <- All_ROC %>% 
  mutate_if(is.numeric, round,2)
All_ROC_round <- All_ROC_round[order(All_ROC_round$AUC, decreasing = TRUE), ]

for(feat_i in 1:length(All_ROC_round$Feature) ){
  feat_here <- All_ROC_round$Feature[feat_i] 
  # True if class as Syn. False if as Ctl.
  # Direction from the hypothesised direction of each metric, not from its AUC rank:
  if(feature_direction_named[[feat_here]] == "moreSyn"){ 
    
    ds_Q[[paste0("pass_",feat_here)]]  <- ds_Q[[feat_here]] >= All_ROC_round$threshold[feat_i]
    
  } else {
    
    ds_Q[[paste0("pass_",feat_here)]]  <- ds_Q[[feat_here]] <= All_ROC_round$threshold[feat_i]
  }
}

```
